editor_spans.body: The Motherwell speech gives the Holyrood offer more substance than the press release suggested. Burnham is not only asking Edinburgh to devolve its own powers. He is offering something Westminster controls: DWP employment support, shaped by Holyrood. He is also floating devolved innovation, enterprise and employability funding, and has called a National Economic Council with the devolved First Ministers. That is a real incentive. It partly answers my earlier point that Westminster had little power to compel anything here. It cannot compel, but it can pay.

The speech has a sound historical diagnosis. Ravenscraig and the Leigh pits were closed by people who never had to live with the consequences, and nobody planned the transition. More than thirty years on, the Ravenscraig site is still not fully filled. Those decisions taught a generation that the state does things to places, not with them. That loss of trust is what Burnham is really trying to repair.

There is a tension at the centre of the plan. Easterhouse worked because it was small, local and personal: tailored pathways, clothes for interviews, travel paid. Burnham now wants to take that model 'nationwide', 'the way we support everybody, everywhere'. Scaling a bottom-up project through a national employment system is exactly how good local practice turns into the top-down, tick-box scheme he condemns in the same speech. The test of the DWP offer is whether the money and discretion reach the estate level, or stop at Holyrood.

The rest of the material is still modest. The flagship example of cooperation is £10 million matched for two defence colleges. Meanwhile one in six young Scots is not in education, employment or training. The procurement idea of paying a little more to buy British, as with Manchester's Falkirk-built buses, is the most radical part of the speech, but it is stated as a wish, not a policy. The warning that Scottish towns could be 'underpowered' while northern English cities power up is a lever on the SNP. It may prove more persuasive than the open hand.
